description_full: AGCO Corporation manufactures and distributes agricultural equipment and replacement parts worldwide. It offers horsepower tractors for row crop production, soil cultivation, planting, land leveling, seeding, and commercial hay operations; utility tractors for small- and medium-sized farms, as well as for dairy, livestock, orchards, and vineyards; and compact tractors for small farms, specialty agricultural industries, landscaping, equestrian, and residential uses. The company also provides grain storage bins and related drying and handling equipment systems; seed-processing systems; swine and poultry feed storage and delivery systems; ventilation and watering systems; and egg production systems and broiler production equipment. In addition, it offers round and rectangular balers, loader wagons, self-propelled windrowers, forage harvesters, disc mowers, spreaders, rakes, tedders, and mower conditioners for harvesting and packaging vegetative feeds used in cattle, dairy, horse, and renewable fuel industries. Further, the company provides implements, including disc harrows leveling seed beds and mixing chemicals with the soils; heavy tillage to break up soil and mix crop residue into topsoil; field cultivators that prepare smooth seed bed and destroy weeds; drills for small grain seeding; planters and other planting equipment; and loaders. Additionally, it offers combines for harvesting grain crops, such as corn, wheat, soybeans, and rice; and application equipment, including self-propelled, three- and four-wheeled vehicles, and related equipment for liquid and dry fertilizers and crop protection chemicals, and for after crops emerge from the ground, as well as produces diesel engines, gears, and generating sets. The company markets its products under the Fendt, Massey Ferguson, PTx, and Valtra brands through a network of independent dealers and distributors. AGCO Corporation was founded in 1990 and is headquartered in Duluth, Georgia.

financial_summary: AGCO Corporation is a mid-cap industrials business with a $7.7B market cap on $10.1B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -7% over the past three years and +3% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.

Returns on capital run at 22% against a 9% cost of capital — a 13-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, and 22% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $740M in free cash flow — roughly 7 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.36× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 1.9× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 25× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 4.4% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 18% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.
